extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: pooled RR for the highest versus the lowest category was 0.98

studies.Reference: Plasma carotenoids, retinol and tocopherol levels and the risk of ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Jeong NH, Song ES, Lee JM, Lee KB, Kim MK, Cheon JE, Lee JK, Son SK, Lee JP, Kim JH, Hur SY, Kwon YI
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Preoperative plasma concentrations of beta-carotene, lycopene, zeaxanthin plus lutein, retinol, alpha-tocopherol, and gamma-tocopherol were measured by reverse-phase, gradient high-pressure liquid chromatography.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Forty-five epithelial ovarian cancers and 135 age-matched controls.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Women with the highest tertiles of retinol (OR 0.45; 95%CI 0.21-0.98) had lower risk of ovarian cancer than women in the lowest tertiles.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Women with the highest tertiles of retinol had lower risk of ovarian cancer than women in the lowest tertiles.
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.042.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Preoperative plasma concentrations of retinol were measured by reverse-phase, gradient high-pressure liquid chromatography.

studies.Reference: A population-based case-control study of carotenoid and vitamin A intake and ovarian cancer (United States).
studies.Authors: Bertone ER, Hankinson SE, Newcomb PA, Rosner B, Willet WC, Stampfer MJ, Egan KM
studies.comparison_type: Highest vs Lowest (≥24,000 µg/week vs lowest intake)
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Data were collected by telephone interview, which included an abbreviated food and supplement list to quantify typical consumption of carotenoids (lutein/zeaxanthin, alpha-carotene, beta-carotene), retinol and total vitamin A at 5 years prior to diagnosis in cases, or to a comparable reference date in controls.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 327 cases and 3129 controls were included in the analysis
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Participants with the highest dietary intake of lutein/zeaxanthin (> or =24,000 microg/week) experienced a 40% lower risk of ovarian cancer
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.048.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Incident cases diagnosed between 1991 and 1994 were identified through statewide tumor registries
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: abbreviated food and supplement list to quantify typical consumption of carotenoids (lutein/zeaxanthin, alpha-carotene, beta-carotene), retinol and total vitamin A

studies.Reference: Risk of ovarian carcinoma and consumption of vitamins A, C, and E and specific carotenoids: a prospective analysis.
studies.Authors: Fairfield KM, Hankinson SE, Rosner BA, Hunter DJ, Colditz GA, Willett WC
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Women reported on known and suspected ovarian carcinoma risk factors including reproductive factors, smoking, and use of vitamin supplements on biennial mailed questionnaires from 1976 to 1996. Food frequency questionnaires were included in 1980, 1984, 1986, and 1990.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 80,326 participants in the Nurses' Health Study who had no history of cancer other than nonmelanoma skin carcinoma
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: The multivariate relative risks (95% confidence intervals [CIs]) for ovarian carcinoma among women in the highest versus lowest quintile of intake were 1.04 (95% CI, 0.72-1.51) for vitamin A from foods and supplements
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: The authors observed no association between ovarian carcinoma risk and antioxidant vitamin consumption from foods, or foods and supplements together.
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.836.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: The authors confirmed 301 incident cases of invasive epithelial ovarian carcinoma during 16 years of dietary follow-up (1980-1996).
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: consumption of vitamins A, C, and E and specific carotenoids, as well as fruit and vegetable intake; vitamin A from foods and supplements

studies.Reference: Intake of vitamins A, C, and E and folate and the risk of ovarian cancer in a pooled analysis of 10 cohort studies.
studies.Authors: Koushik A, Wang M, Anderson KE, van den Brandt P, Clendenen TV, Eliassen AH, Freudenheim JL, Genkinger JM, Håkansson N, Marshall JR, McCullough ML, Miller AB, Robien K, Rohan TE, Schairer C, Schouten LJ, Tworoger SS, Wang Y, Wolk A, Zeleniuch-Jacquotte A, Smith-Warner SA
studies.comparison_type: per 1,300 mcg/day increase in total vitamin A intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Vitamin intakes were estimated from validated food frequency questionnaires in each study.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Among 501,857 women, 1,973 cases of ovarian cancer occurred over a median follow-up period of 7-16 years across studies.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: The pooled multivariate RRs [95% confidence intervals (CIs)] for incremental increases in total intake of each vitamin were 1.02 (0.97-1.07) for vitamin A (increment: 1,300 mcg/day)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Dietary and total intakes of each vitamin were not significantly associated with ovarian cancer risk.
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: not significantly associated Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.429.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: total (food and supplemental) vitamin intake; vitamin A (increment: 1,300 mcg/day)

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.2415). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 7 studies yielded an effect size of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.83–1.08), indicating no statistically significant association between vitamin_a and ovarian cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 61.72%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
